Restoration of America Foundation | 153 Fort Wade Road, Suite 250 | Ponte Vedra, FL 32081 
September 3, 2025 
 
Dr. Steven L. Lieberman 
Acting Under Secretary for Health 
Department of Veterans Affairs 
810 Vermont Avenue NW 
Washington, DC 20420 
Subject: Comment on proposed rule related to 38 CFR Part 17  
RIN 2900-AS31 
Dear Dr. Lieberman, 
Restoration of America Foundation is a 501(c)(3) entity which focuses on public policy efforts to 
protect life at all stages, restore the military to the world's most dominant fighting force, and 
educate our younger generations and new Americans on the U.S. Constitution. 
We write in strong support of the Department of Veterans Affairs’ (VA) proposed rule to fully 
exclude abortion benefits and abortion counseling from the medical benefits provided by the 
Department. The previous rule, made interim in 2022 and final in 2024 under the Biden 
Administration, violated the statute and overturned over 25 years of regulatory interpretation that 
previously excluded these services from the Veterans Health Administration (VHA) programs. 
We believe that proposed rule RIN 2900-AS31 realigns VA health services for veterans and their 
families with statute, congressional intent, the American public’s preferences, and sound health 
policy.  
First, the Biden Administration’s rule change appears to be a politically motivated scheme to 
undermine laws in Republican-led states that sought to protect unborn life following the Dobbs v. 
Jackson Women’s Health Supreme Court decision in 2022. The Interim Final Rule (IFR) that the 
Department of Veterans Affairs posted in September of 2022 opens with a summary of the Dobbs 
case and acknowledges that the rule change is motivated by a desire to extend abortion rights 
into states with legal restrictions.1  Further, the IFR creates a “health of the mother” exception, 
which in practice means a right to fully elective abortion given the expansive definition of 
“health” applied to abortion laws in the past. Per the Supreme Court’s opinion in Doe v. Bolton 
(1973), “[T]he medical judgment may be exercised in the light of all factors—physical, 
emotional, psychological, familial, and the woman's age—relevant to the well-being of the 
patient.”2 Any pregnancy could be considered as affecting the mother’s health under that 
 
1 “AR57-Interim Final Rule - Reproductive Health Services.” Regulations.Gov, Department of Veterans Affairs, 
September 9, 2022, www.regulations.gov/document/VA-2022-VHA-0021-0001.  
2 Doe v. Bolton, 410 U.S. 179 (1973), accessed September 2, 2025: https://tile.loc.gov/storage-
services/service/ll/usrep/usrep410/usrep410179/usrep410179.pdf.  

 
 
Restoration of America Foundation | 153 Fort Wade Road, Suite 250 | Ponte Vedra, FL 32081 
definition. The previous administration’s openness about its motivations casts doubt on the 
sincerity of the IFR’s legal reasoning at the outset and colors its attempt to stretch existing law to 
insert an entitlement to abortion where none exists. 
Federal law explicitly excludes the provision of abortion care under Section 106 of the Veterans 
Health Care Act of 1992.3 It is our view that the Biden Administration, in its previous 
rulemaking, asserted legal ambiguity on the question of VHA coverage of elective abortion 
where there is none. In August of 2021, Senator Moran reiterated this position in a press release,4 
which included a reference to the VA acknowledging this statutory limitation on its own website, 
and we agree with his analysis and conclusion that it is unlawful for the VA to provide abortion 
services. The proposed rule, in undoing the previous rulemaking, would simply align the 
regulatory interpretation with standing law.  
Given that the VHA did not provide abortions at any point in its history until 2022, it is a stretch 
of the imagination to conclude that the Congresses that passed the Veterans Health Care Act of 
1992 or the Veterans’ Health Care Eligibility Reform Act of 1996 intended for elective abortion 
to be a covered service. The fact that the VA explicitly excluded abortion services from the 
medical benefits package in 1999 rulemaking5 and was never corrected by Congress, either 
through passage of an amendment to the law or any other action, further supports the claim that 
Congress did not intend to cover abortion. The explicit language of the 1992 law, in the context 
of Congress’s action or lack of action afterward, contradicts the Biden Administration’s claim 
that there was legal ambiguity on the question of whether Congress intended the VHA to cover 
abortion services.  
Polling has consistently shown that Americans oppose taxpayer funding for abortions. A January 
2025 Marist Poll revealed that 57 percent of respondents oppose or strongly oppose taxpayer 
funding for abortions.6 This is in line with previous poll results, which have shown a consistent 
opposition to taxpayer funding for abortion. This also aligns with the Hyde Amendment, 
restricting federal funding for abortions in annual appropriations for the Departments of Labor, 
Health and Human Services, and Education, which has been in effect since 1977 and has been 
included in every federal appropriations process in spite of changes in party control of Congress 
and the presidency.7

Restoration of America Foundation | 153 Fort Wade Road, Suite 250 | Ponte Vedra, FL 32081 
Lastly, the proposed rule is good health policy and aligns with the mission of the Veterans Health 
Administration (VHA). The stated mission of the VHA is to “Honor America’s Veterans by 
providing exceptional health care that improves their health and well-being.”8 As an organization 
invested in the readiness and integrity of the U.S. military, we have an interest in ensuring the 
fair treatment of our nation’s veterans. For this reason, we believe that veterans’ health benefits 
should be geared towards maintaining and improving the health of patients under its system, 
rather than facilitating the destruction of unborn human lives. Health care should be oriented 
towards the preservation of life and should abstain from harming the patient, including an unborn 
patient, in line with the original Hippocratic Oath.9  
While the harms of abortion to the unborn child are obvious, the VA should also consider the 
risks that abortion poses to the health of the mother. It has been well established that there are 
physical risks of surgical abortion to the mother10 and to future pregnancies.11  Perhaps more 
urgently, a recent Restoration of America Foundation study of medical claims data indicated that 
more than 1 in 10 women experienced a serious adverse event following the use of the chemical 
abortion pill mifepristone.12 Serious events included (but were not limited to) transfusion, sepsis, 
ER visit, hospitalization related to medical abortion, infection without sepsis, and hemorrhage.13 
It is not in the best interest of our female veterans to cover a risky elective procedure.  
We strongly support the proposed rule to exclude abortion services from Veterans Affairs health 
programs and ensure that the Department remains focused on high-quality health services for our 
nation’s veterans and their families. Thank you in advance for your consideration.  
Respectfully,  
 
Doug Truax 
Founder and CEO 
Restoration of America Foundation
